Introduction to Electromagnetic Induction

This lesson explains the step-by-step process of how electromagnetic induction occurs, which is the fundamental principle behind generators and many electrical devices.

START
2 of 6
Step 1
Setup and Motion

Start with a coil of wire and a magnet. Move the magnet toward or away from the coil, or move the coil in the magnetic field.

3 of 6
Step 2
Changing Magnetic Flux

The movement causes the amount of magnetic field passing through the coil (magnetic flux) to change.

4 of 6
Step 3
Induced Voltage Appears

The change in magnetic flux creates a voltage across the ends of the coil. This is called the induced voltage.

5 of 6
Step 4
Current Flows in Circuit

If the coil is part of a closed circuit, the induced voltage pushes charges, creating an electric current that flows through the wire.

6 of 6
Summary of Electromagnetic Induction

Whenever the magnetic environment of a coil changes, a voltage is induced, and if the circuit is complete, current will flow. This is the basic process behind generators and many other devices.

Worked example: Calculate an induced voltage

A 100-turn coil has area 0.020 m² per turn. A uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the coil grows from 0.10 T to 0.30 T in 0.50 s. Find average induced EMF. The complete circuit has resistance 10 Ω.

START
2 of 6
Step 1
Calculate flux change per turn

Magnetic flux is field times area when the field is perpendicular to the coil. The given area is for one turn, so do not multiply by the turn count yet.

3 of 6
Step 2
Apply Faraday’s law

Average EMF magnitude equals the turn count times flux change per turn divided by the elapsed time.

4 of 6
Step 3
Use Lenz’s law for direction

An increasing field into the page induces a field out of the page. The right-hand rule gives counterclockwise current as viewed here. For negligible self-inductance, divide EMF by total resistance.

5 of 6
Step 4
Test the rate of change

The same flux change in half the time produces twice the average EMF. Once the field becomes steady, induced EMF from this changing external field is zero.

6 of 6
Check the complete result

Average induced EMF is 0.80 V and the resistive-circuit current is 0.080 A. Induced current opposes the change in flux, not necessarily the existing field.
